Title: Identifying Non-Ideal Reaction-Diffusion Systems Unable to Maintain Diffusion Out-of-Equilibrium

URL Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06030v1

Published Time: Wed, 08 Jul 2026 00:45:00 GMT

Number of Pages: 9

Markdown Content:
Identifying Non-Ideal Reaction-Diffusion Systems Unable to Maintain Diffusion Out-of-Equilibrium 

Francesco Avanzini, 1, ∗ Timur Aslyamov, 2, † and Massimiliano Esposito 2, ‡

> 1

Department of Chemical Sciences, University of Padova, Via F. Marzolo, 1, I-35131 Padova, Italy 

> 2

Complex Systems and Statistical Mechanics, Department of Physics and Materials Science, University of Luxembourg, 30 Avenue des Hauts-Fourneaux, L-4362 Esch-sur-Alzette, Luxembourg 

(Dated: July 8, 2026) We develop a general method, based on the construction of a kinetic potential acting as a Lyapunov function, to establish when diffusion necessarily equilibrates in non-ideal reaction-diffusion systems, under arbitrary driving by autonomous homogeneous chemostats. Using this method, we generalize the results of J. Chem. Phys. 161 , 174108 (2024) by relaxing some of the underlying assumptions. Specifically, we show that diffusion equilibrates in reaction-diffusion systems whose chemical reaction network is either pseudo-detailed balanced, with reaction fluxes controlled by the stoichiometry of reactants and products, or complex balanced, with reaction fluxes controlled only by the stoichiometry of the reactants. The different constraints on the reaction fluxes are shown to originate from the distinct stoichiometric properties of the two classes of networks. 

I. INTRODUCTION 

Self-organization of molecules is ubiquitous in nature, giv-ing rise to complex spatio-temporal structures. This phe-nomenon has gained renewed attention following the discov-ery of biomolecular condensates in cells [1–3]: membrane-less compartments, resulting from liquid-liquid phase sepa-ration and serving a wide range of biological functions [4– 7]. Indeed, understanding the physical principles underlying the formation and regulation of such condensates remains challenging. In contrast to equilibrium self-organization [8], which is governed solely by molecular interactions and dif-fusion, biomolecular condensates arise in complex environ-ments, where their constituents are involved in chemical re-actions that are continuously driven out of equilibrium. Recently, significant efforts have been devoted to eluci-dating these physical principles using complementary ap-proaches. Microscopic, particle-based approaches have been used to investigate molecular-scale effects, such as crowd-ing [9], the frequency of molecular encounters [10], and in-terfacial phenomena [11, 12]. Mesoscopic, mean-field ap-proaches have been extensively developed to investigate a wide range of phenomena [13, 14]. These include, but are not limited to, the emergence of specific spatial concentra-tion profiles [15–18], and their regulation by chemical reac-tions [19–22] and molecular interactions [23]; the nature of instabilities of the homogeneous phase [24]; the factors con-trolling coarsening of self-organized structures [25–28]; and the role of condensates as microreactors regulating chemical reactions [29]. These advances have been instrumental in shaping our current understanding of biomolecular condensates. Never-theless, many existing approaches rely on phenomenologi-cal descriptions that do not systematically enforce thermody-namic consistency, thereby limiting the identification of gen-eral principles governing nonequilibrium self-organization.

To address this limitation, we developed in a previous work [30] a thermodynamically consistent mean-field the-ory for open, non-ideal reaction-diffusion systems, by com-bining thermodynamic frameworks for non-ideal chemical reaction networks [31, 32] and ideal reaction-diffusion sys-tems [33, 34]. Within this framework, we identified classes of chemical reaction networks (i.e., pseudo-detailed balanced and complex balanced) for which diffusion cannot be sus-tained out of equilibrium, irrespective of the strength of the nonequilibrium driving by autonomous homogeneous chemostats. These results were derived for arbitrary molec-ular interactions and under specific assumptions on the re-action fluxes, although the underlying physical mechanism was expected to be more general. This broader expectation, however, appeared to clash with particle-based simulations of reaction-diffusion systems with pseudo-detailed balanced networks, where diffusion was observed to remain out of equilibrium [9, 12]. To understand this apparent contradiction, we develop a general method whose central ingredient is the construction of a kinetic potential acting as a Lyapunov function. The method establishes when diffusion necessarily equilibrates and is applied to both pseudo-detailed balanced and complex balanced networks. This allows us to identify the fundamen-tal conditions that reaction fluxes must satisfy for diffusion to equilibrate within these two classes of networks. On the one hand, reaction fluxes in pseudo-detailed balanced chemical reaction networks must be controlled by the stoichiometry of potentially both reactants and products, as formally specified by Eq. (22). In Ref. [30], we instead considered reaction fluxes controlled by the stoichiometry of the reactants only. On the other hand, reaction fluxes in complex balanced chem-ical reaction networks need only be controlled by the stoi-chiometry of the reactants, as formally specified by Eq. (37). In Ref. [30], we instead considered Arrhenius-like reaction fluxes only. When reaction fluxes do not satisfy these condi-tions, as in Refs. [9, 12], diffusion can instead be maintained out of equilibrium. Furthermore, the method reveals the con-ditions leading to a novel lower bound on the entropy pro-duction rate due to reactions. The paper is organized as follows. Section II summarizes the main setup for the mean-field dynamic and thermody-arXiv:2607.06030v1 [cond-mat.stat-mech] 7 Jul 2026 2namic description of reaction-diffusion systems. Section III introduces the two classes of chemical reaction networks based on their topological properties. Section IV derives our results, which are then discussed and compared with other results in the literature in Sec. V.

> III. TOPOLOGICAL CLASSIFICATION OF CRNS

Here we introduce two classes of CRNs, based on the topo-logical properties of cycles , complexes , and lumped reactions .

> V. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS

We have developed a method, based on the construction of a kinetic potential acting as a Lyapunov function, to establish when diffusion equilibrates in RD systems with autonomous homogeneous chemostatting. We have applied this method to show that diffusion equilibrates in systems with either pseudo-detailed balanced or complex balanced CRNs. When diffusion equilibrates, according to Eq. (8b), the chemical po-tentials become homogeneous, ∇𝜇 𝑖 (𝒄 ss (𝒓 )) = 0, and diffusion currents vanish, 𝑱 𝑖 (𝒄 ss (𝒓 )) = 0. This has been proven under the assumption that reaction fluxes satisfy mild class-specific constraints. In particular, they must satisfy Eqs. (22) and (37) for pseudo-detailed bal-anced and complex balanced CRNs, respectively. Notably, the constraints imposed on the reaction fluxes for complex balanced CRNs are more restrictive than those for pseudo-detailed balanced CRNs: all fluxes satisfying Eq. (37) also sat-isfy Eq. (22), whereas the converse does not generally hold. This difference originates from the different stoichiometric properties of the two classes underpinning the proofs pre-sented in Sec. IV. In pseudo-detailed balanced CRNs, the crucial ingredient of the proof is that {𝑏 𝜀 } are constant. According to Eq. (33), this requires that the terms depending on the dynamical con-centrations, entering the sums in both the numerator and de-nominator of each 𝑏 𝜀 through {𝑠 |𝜌 | (𝒄 (𝒓 ))} with 𝜌 ∈ R 𝜀 , can-cel out. Therefore, this condition only allows for reaction fluxes whose dependence on the dynamical concentrations is determined solely by the lumped reaction 𝜀 and not by the specific reaction 𝜌 .In complex balanced CRNs, the crucial ingredient of the proof is that the steady-state condition Í𝜌 >0 𝜕 𝜅,𝜌 𝑗 𝜌 (𝒄 hss ) = 0can be rewritten as in Eq. (44), where the functional depen-dence on the concentrations appears only through the ex-ponential terms. This rewriting requires factorizing out the fluxes of all reactions having the complex 𝜅 as a reactant. Therefore, it only allows for reaction fluxes whose depen-dence on the dynamical concentrations is determined solely by the complex 𝜅 and not by the specific reaction 𝜌 . This directly yields the steady-state condition in Eq. (43). When the reaction fluxes do not satisfy Eq. (22) for pseudo-detailed balanced CRNs or Eq. (37) for complex balanced CRNs, diffusion can be maintained out of equilibrium even under homogeneous chemostatting, and the chemical po-tentials of the internal species become non-homogeneous at steady state. This has, for instance, been observed in the illustration presented in Ref. [41], where a pseudo-detailed balanced CRN with a single lumped reaction was consid-ered within a mean-field approach. There, different reactions within the same lumped reaction depend on the local total density in different ways. Specifically, the transition rates 

{𝑘 ±𝜌 } entering the fluxes in Eq. (25) for reactions involving chemostatted species increase linearly with the total concen-tration 𝒄 tot (𝒓 ) of internal species: 𝑘 ±𝜌 ∝ ( 1 +𝜁 𝒄 tot (𝒓 )) , where the parameter 𝜁 controls the dependence on the total con-centration. Conversely, the transition rates {𝑘 ±𝜌 } entering the fluxes in Eq. (25) for reactions not involving chemostat-ted species remain constant. As a result, the concentration dependence of the reaction fluxes is not determined solely by the lumped reaction. Consequently, Eq. (22) is not sat-isfied and the steady-state chemical potentials of the inter-nal species are non-homogeneous. A similar behavior has also been observed in Refs. [9, 44], where a pseudo-detailed balanced CRN with a single lumped reaction was consid-ered within a particle-based approach under similar assump-tions: reactions involving chemostatted species dominate in the dense phase, while reactions not involving chemostatted species dominate in the dilute phase. Beyond pseudo-detailed balanced and complex balanced CRNs, a general procedure to construct ˆ 𝐹 [𝒄 ] whose corre-sponding ˆ¤Π[𝒄 ] is non-negative is still lacking. Whether such a general procedure exists, or whether the construction is in-herently network-specific, remains an open question that we leave to future work.
